articles.title: Distinct brain network organization in asynchronous and synchronous motor observation and motor imagery: evidence from EEG functional connectivity, phase-amplitude coupling, and decoding
articles.content:
Publication date: 1 November 2026

Source: NeuroImage, Volume 341

Author(s): Tingting Lian, Ming Tang, Rui Zhao, Yixin Zhang, Jinxiang Zhang, Cheng Cheng, Jiahui Han

articles.title: Optimizing Intermittent Theta-Burst Stimulation: The Effects of Pulse Parameters on Corticospinal Excitability
articles.content: Objective. Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) is a repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) protocol used in clinical settings to alleviate symptoms of psychiatric disorders. Although the pulse parameters currently used in iTBS have remained unchanged since the first treatments, recent controllable TMS devices allow for the personalization of pulse shape and duration, opening the possibility of testing the efficacy of other pulse parameters in modulating corticospinal excitability (CSE). Methods. In a repeated-measures design, changes in CSE were induced by the administration of iTBS over the left primary motor cortex under three different conditions: long bidirectional pulse (L-Bi), long quasi-unidirectional pulse (L-QU), and a control short quasi-unidirectional pulse (S-QU). We assessed TMS-induced motor evoked potentials before and up to 70 minutes after iTBS. We hypothesized that L-QU pulses would induce greater facilitation than other conditions. Results. A mixed linear model showed that all conditions induced increased MEPs compared to baseline. However, the L-Bi pulse led to a larger and more sustained MEP increase than both unidirectional pulses, while the S-QU pulse appeared less effective in modulating CSE. We observed large within- and between-subject variability in responsiveness to the iTBS protocols. Conclusion. These results suggest that L-Bi pulses in iTBS protocols are more potent than unidirectional pulses in inducing CSE changes in the cortex of healthy adults. The individual variability in response to iTBS and the potential clinical relevance of these findings are discussed.
articles.author: Proulx, B., Hasani, S. A., Frechette, A.-J., Hamel, R., Tremblay, S., Cote, S., Lepage, J.-F.

articles.title: Suzetrigine-evoked analgesia is potentiated by Nav1.7 null-related opioid mechanisms.
articles.content: The genetic evidence for an essential role of sodium channel Nav1.7 in human pain conditions is compelling. Unfortunately, potent selective channel blockers of Nav1.7 are not useful analgesics because they have deleterious side effects, particularly on the autonomic nervous system. Here we have evaluated the downstream mechanisms induced by Nav1.7 loss in utero. Nav1.1 compensates for loss of Nav1.7 in sensory neurons and antisense Nav1.1 oligonucleotides diminish excitability in Nav1.7 embryonic null sensory neurons. Enhanced endogenous opioid signalling contributes substantially to analgesia. This is linked to altered gene expression that potentiates opioid signalling through lowered levels of proteins that terminate G-protein signalling (RGS4 and RGS8). There is also enhanced opioid drive through increased enkephalin levels linked to lowered sodium levels in Nav1.7 null neurons. Opioid signalling is the main driver of analgesia, but enhanced potassium channel expression (KCNC4 KCNK2, KCNMB2, KCNAB3) all implicated in pain control, may also contribute to the small level of naloxone-resistant analgesia. These findings suggest a potential new route to analgesia, through mimicking the events at Nav1.7 null sensory neuron terminals. Here we demonstrate potentiation of suzetrigine-evoked analgesia with RGS antagonists alone or in combination with normally inactive doses of morphine in formalin-evoked pain and CFA-induced inflammatory pain. Intriguingly, no analgesia is observed with acute pain. Cancer pain is under investigation. These data are of potential clinical interest.
articles.author: Riquelme, E. V., Didenko, O., Gossage, S., Isensee, J., Hucho, T., wood, j.

articles.title: Sustained Activation of a Defensive Behavior-Related Circuit Elicits a distinct Homeostatic Sleep Response
articles.content: Animals and humans often forgo sleep in response to other physiological needs. Prolonged wakefulness leads to a compensatory homeostatic sleep response involving enhanced amounts of sleep and electroencephalographic delta (0.5-4 Hz) power, yet how the type of preceding wakefulness and brain activity affects this response is poorly understood. Here we compared the pattern of brain activity and the homeostatic sleep response following sustained wakefulness induced by either gentle handling (GH), a widely used form of sleep deprivation in rodents; or optogenetic stimulation of neurons involved in avoidance/defensive responses, basal forebrain (BF) vesicular glutamatergic transporter type 2 (vGluT2) neurons. Local infusion of ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists partially attenuated the wake-inducing effect of vGluT2-stimulation, but not that of GH, suggesting mediation by other non-glutamatergic BF subtypes. These antagonists also tended to produce more NREM sleep and a shorter NREM latency in the recovery period following vGluT2-stimulation. Both manipulations increased high theta (7-9 Hz) during wakefulness, an effect partially blocked by local infusion of the glutamate antagonist cocktail. Enhanced NREM sleep time and NREM delta power in the recovery period were more pronounced following GH than following vGluT2 stimulation. Whole-brain cFos immunohistochemistry revealed stronger neuronal activity in brain regions involved in stress and avoidance/defensive behaviors with vGluT2 stimulation, compared to GH. Our results demonstrate that activation of a brain system involved in defensive behavior (BF vGluT2) elicits a distinct and diminished homeostatic sleep response compared to GH, potentially an evolutionary sleep adaptation which would maintain vigilance in the face of an ongoing threat.
articles.author: Yang, C., Lombardi, V., Uygun, D. S., Brown, R. E., McKenna, J. T., Basheer, R.

articles.title: NE52-QQ57 attenuates post-ischemia protein phosphorylation in the mouse brain
articles.content: Introduction: Cerebral ischemia induces a reduction in brain pH. GPR4, a proton-sensing G protein-coupled receptor is highly expressed in vascular endothelial cells. Pharmacological inhibition of GPR4 with NE52-QQ57 (NEQQ) reduces ischemia-induced blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption and brain injury. To facilitate targeting GPR4 in vivo, it is important to better define the effect of NEQQ on post-ischemia signaling and the pharmacokinetics of NEQQ in vivo. Methods: We performed biochemical analysis following transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO). We used Liquid Chromatography-Mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) to quantify the concentration of NEQQ in serum, brain, and peripheral tissues. Results: NEQQ administration decreased the phosphorylation of PKA substrates, PKC substrates, ERK1/2, and CREB. LC-MS/MS analysis detected NEQQ in both ipsilateral and contralateral hemisphere of the brain at 5 h and 24 h after reperfusion, demonstrating that NEQQ crosses the BBB. In peripheral tissues, NEQQ exhibited highest level in kidney and lowest in the heart. In sham controls, average serum concentrations were ~4 and 0.9 g/g at 5 and 24 h, respectively. Following tMCAO, ipsilateral brain exhibited higher levels as compared to the contralateral side at 5 h while the difference diminished at 24 h. Conclusions: NEQQ attenuated the ischemia-induced activation of multiple signaling pathways. NEQQ exhibited broad distribution in peripheral organs, and its brain level was sufficient for GPR4 inhibition at 24 h after injection. These findings support the use of NEQQ as a pharmacological inhibitor of GPR4-mediated signaling following ischemic stroke.
articles.author: Joshi, S., Zhou, Y., Zha, X.-m.

articles.title: Therapeutic AIBP expression contributes to synaptic preservation and vision restoration against glaucomatous neuroinflammation
articles.content: Lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) is the only approved treatment for glaucoma, yet retinal ganglion cell (RGC) degeneration and vision loss often progress despite reducing IOP. Apolipoprotein A-I binding protein (AIBP) stabilizes ATP-binding cassette subfamily A member 1 (ABCA1) and promotes cholesterol efflux, thus controlling cholesterol-rich lipid rafts and restraining lipid raft-dependent Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) inflammatory signaling. Here we show that AAV2-mediated expression of human AIBP (hAIBP) preserves inner retinal synaptic integrity and visual function in experimental glaucoma without altering IOP. In DBA/2J mice, a single intravitreal injection of AAV2-hAIBP at 5 months protected RGCs and preserved pattern electroretinogram and pattern visual evoked potential responses at 10 months, even though IOP was indistinguishable from empty-vector controls. AAV2-hAIBP preserved CaMKII and synapsin phosphorylation, restored synaptophysin and PSD95 in the inner plexiform layer, and reduced the expression of TLR4, complement C1q, IBA1, IL-1b, and IL-6 induction in Muller glia and microglia. Comparable protection was observed in microbead-induced ocular hypertension in C57BL/6 mice, both when the AAV2-hAIBP was delivered before microbead injection and when it was delivered after IOP elevation was established. Elevated IOP reduced endogenous retinal AIBP and ABCA1 expression, and AAV2-hAIBP restored both. Protection required the TLR4-binding domain, as an AIBP mutant lacking this domain failed to preserve RGCs. Conversely, AIBP knockout retinas exhibited increased CaMKII phosphorylation and reduced synaptophysin in the absence of elevated IOP. These findings identify synaptic preservation through the AIBP-TLR4 axis as an IOP-independent therapeutic mechanism and support AAV2-hAIBP as a candidate gene therapy for glaucoma.
articles.author: Bastola, T., Hwang, S., Shen, Z., Choi, S.-H., Choi, S., Jang, E., Poudel, M., Kim, K.-Y., Miller, Y. I., Weinreb, R. N., Ju, W.-K.

articles.title: From Intrinsic Topography to Cognitive Prediction: Benchmarking Approaches to Personalized Cortical Parcellation
articles.content: Personalized functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) adapts cortical parcellations to individual functional anatomy. Various methods have been proposed that differ in how they combine group-level information, spatial constraints, and individual functional data. Using the Human Connectome Project Young Adult dataset (N = 947), we compared five personalized parcellation methods and a standard group-level atlas. For each method, we calculated functional homogeneity, test-retest reliability, parcel contiguity, and inter-individual Dice overlap. Personalized parcellation methods generally yielded higher functional homogeneity and lower inter-individual Dice than the group atlas, while test-retest reliability of functional connectivity was high across methods. Parcel contiguity differed across methods: some approaches produced almost entirely contiguous parcels, whereas others frequently produced spatially disconnected components, indicating that the detection of candidate ectopic variants depends partly on the parcellation strategy. We also examined whether connectivity and topographic features were associated with and predicted general intelligence (g). Using structural equation modeling, intra-individual parcel size variability and inter-individual parcel size similarity derived from the hierarchical Bayesian method (gMSHBM) were positively associated with g, whereas no corresponding association survived correction for the other methods. Using kernel ridge regression, functional connectivity significantly predicted g, with the group atlas yielding the highest predictive accuracy, consistent with a potential advantage of cross-individual spatial correspondence for edge-wise prediction. Finally, we assessed robustness across four preprocessing pipelines. Although gMSHBM parcellations were not re-estimated, relative between-method patterns in several spatial characteristics were largely preserved. In contrast, brain-behavior associations involving time-series-derived features varied substantially with preprocessing, whereas parcel-size associations were more stable. We conclude that personalized parcellation approaches are associated with distinct trade-offs in spatial correspondence, topographic variability, and downstream predictive utility. The choice of parcellation strategy therefore affects both the properties of individualized maps and the brain-behavior information derived from them.
articles.author: Inceler, Y. C., Burkhardt, M., Giessing, C., Kristanto, D.

articles.title: Neuropeptide Signaling Promotes Stem-Cell Driven Regeneration in Planarians
articles.content: Neurons and neuroendocrine cells produce neuropeptides, which act as long-range signals to modulate organismal state and physiological function. In a few cases, neuropeptides have been thought to promote regeneration, but understanding this connection has been difficult due to the relatively poor regenerative capacity of most traditional model organisms. To test whether neuropeptides drive robust regeneration, we used the highly regenerative asexual planarian flatworm as a model. We began by investigating enzymes that cleave and process pre-propeptides to produce bioactive neuropeptides. We characterized 12 putative neuropeptide-processing enzymes and identified three enzymes, prohormone convertase 2 (pc2), carboxypeptidase E (CPE), and peptidylglycine alpha-hydroxylating monooxygenase (PHM-1) that regulate regeneration through their effects on stem cell differentiation and maintenance. We then investigated 51 of the 52 known neuropeptide-encoding genes in planarians, finding that 16 of these genes promote efficient regeneration and/or stem cell function. Our work indicates that diverse neuropeptides regulate endogenous pluripotent stem cells during homeostasis and in robust regeneration. Our data supports a key role for neuropeptide signaling in planarians to promote a pro-regenerative state, which could be valuable to mimic in regenerative therapies.
articles.author: Endara-Arnold, C. E., Jenkins, J. E., Villalobos, A. E., Roberts-Galbraith, R. H.

articles.title: Acoustic Context Shapes Cortical Encoding of Spectral Discrimination in Normal and Impaired Hearing
articles.content: The auditory change complex (ACC) provides a cortical measure of acoustic discrimination, yet the mechanisms shaping responses to spectrotemporally complex sounds remain poorly understood. We investigated how acoustic context and temporal-envelope variability influence cortical encoding of spectral contrast in normal-hearing (NH) and hearing-impaired (HI) listeners. Electroencephalography (EEG) was used to record ACCs and auditory steady-state responses (ASSRs) evoked by spectrotemporally modulated stimuli. We compared conventional spectro-temporal modulations (STMs) with a novel discrete spectro-temporal modulation (DSTM) paradigm, examined temporal roving, and evaluated cortical responses to spectral contrast in NH and HI listeners. ACCs elicited by DSTM stimuli were larger and more symmetrical across transition directions than those elicited by conventional STMs. Temporal roving markedly reduced responses to intensity changes while largely preserving responses to spectral changes, indicating a partial dissociation between intensity-driven and spectrally driven cortical discrimination. ACC responses decreased systematically with spectral contrast and were weaker and delayed in HI listeners. By contrast, ASSRs remained highly detectable and showed no systematic dependence on spectral contrast, supporting a distinction between contrast-sensitive cortical discrimination and ongoing envelope encoding. Temporal roving further enhanced separation between NH and HI listeners. ACC response strength was significantly associated with behavioural STM discrimination thresholds and explained variance beyond age and audiometric thresholds. These findings demonstrate that cortical representations of spectral discrimination are shaped by acoustic context and temporal-envelope statistics. Temporal roving attenuates intensity-driven responses while preserving spectrally driven discrimination, providing insight into cortical encoding of spectrotemporal contrast and its relationship to perceptual performance.
articles.author: Undurraga Lucero, J. A., Stefancu, I., Rekswinkel, M., Simonsen, L. B., Van Eeckhoutte, M.

articles.title: 5-HT1A Antagonist WAY-100635 Prevents Chronic Neurodegeneration and Immune Activation After TBI
articles.content: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) initiates secondary neurodegeneration that compromises interconnected neural circuits and contributes to persistent visual and neurobehavioral impairment. Pharmacological strategies that preserve vulnerable neurons and synapses while limiting chronic neuroinflammation remain an unmet therapeutic need. We previously identified the serotonin 1A receptor (5-HT1A) antagonist WAY-100635 through screening human stem cell-derived retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and demonstrated that it promotes neuroprotection through cyclic adenosine monophosphate-dependent mitochondrial biogenesis. Here, we investigated whether post-injury treatment extends this neuroprotective efficacy to cerebral and visual circuitry following TBI. Male C57BL/6J mice aged 2-3 months underwent unilateral controlled cortical impact (CCI) involving the left visual cortex. Mice were randomly assigned to sham, untreated injury or treated injury groups, with 3-10 sham controls and 5-8 mice per injury group across experiments. WAY-100635 was administered intraperitoneally at 5 mg/kg daily, beginning 1 hour after injury and continuing for 6 weeks. Therapeutic efficacy was assessed using motor and psychological-health-relevant risk-taking/behavioral disinhibition by elevated-plus-maze assessment, visual electrophysiology, optokinetic responses, diffusion magnetic resonance imaging, and retinal and cortical histopathology. Unilateral cortical injury produced bilateral RGC dysfunction and loss, with greater degeneration in the eye contralateral to the injured hemisphere, consistent with predominantly crossed murine visual projections. WAY-100635 significantly preserved RGC survival and function, improved visual acuity and contrast sensitivity, and preserved visually evoked cortical responses to contralateral eye stimulation. Diffusion MRI revealed bilateral visual pathway abnormalities, with treatment selectively normalizing fractional anisotropy and radial kurtosis in the optic tract ipsilateral to cortical injury. In perilesional cortex, treatment preserved neuronal cell bodies and synapses detected by synaptophysin immunoreactivity while markedly reducing microglial/macrophage activation and reactive astrogliosis. These effects were accompanied by improved early motor performance and attenuation of injury-associated increases in open-arm exploration in the elevated plus maze. Cortical cavity volume was not significantly reduced, supporting preferential protection of vulnerable circuitry surrounding and connected to the primary lesion. These findings identify post-injury WAY-100635 treatment as a novel therapeutic intervention that combines neuronal and synaptic preservation with reduced chronic glial activation and improved functional outcomes. They support further translational development of serotonin 1A receptor antagonism to limit secondary neurodegeneration and the visual and neurobehavioral consequences of TBI.
articles.author: Das, A., Dutta, S., Pradhan, L. K., Chen, J., Wang, N., Gao, X.

articles.title: How aging reshapes implicit learning: behavioral and oscillatory evidence from an EEG-adapted Fast Mapping paradigm.
articles.content: Most of everyday memory formation occurs without deliberate intent, yet the neural mechanisms supporting implicit encoding and their reorganization with age remain poorly understood. The present study investigated age-related changes in implicit learning using an EEG-adapted Fast Mapping paradigm (the Disjunctive Inference Implicit Learning Test, DIILT) in 31 younger and 35 older adults, paired with a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment and a one-month delayed recognition measure. Behaviorally, younger adults rapidly acquired novel implicit associations across the learning phase, whereas older adults showed persistent reliance on familiar items and limited improvement for novel associations. Critically, both groups successfully retained novel associations after one month, with implicitly learned associations showing greater long-term stability than explicitly encoded ones regardless of age. At the neural level, younger adults exhibited early posterior theta engagement for novel compared to familiar items, which disappeared by the end of learning, consistent with novelty-driven associative encoding. Older adults showed no such theta modulation for novel items, pointing to reorganization of the neural mechanisms supporting implicit encoding. Theta dynamics predicted immediate recognition in younger adults but not in older adults who rather showed theta association with processing speed, suggesting an age-related shift from memory-specific binding to domain-general cognitive resource allocation, consistent with neural maintenance frameworks of cognitive aging. These findings demonstrate that implicit encoding produces durable memory traces across the lifespan but relies on reorganized oscillatory dynamics in aging, with implications for understanding how cognitive aging reshapes everyday memory formation.
